question: What are the three types of tests in Flutter and when to use each?
answer:
Flutter has three test layers that trade speed against confidence: unit, widget, and integration.

The pyramid shape is the point — many fast unit tests, fewer widget tests, a handful of integration tests.

Unit tests — fastest, most numerous:
• One function, class or method in isolation
• Dependencies replaced by fakes or mocks
• Plain `test()` from package:test; no Flutter engine needed

Widget tests — medium speed, medium coverage:
• One widget or a small tree, rendered headlessly on a fake clock
• `testWidgets()` plus WidgetTester; tap, drag, enter text, pump frames
• The sweet spot for screen logic — no device, still real rendering

Integration tests — slowest, fewest, highest confidence:
• The whole app on a real device or emulator via the integration_test package (or patrol when native dialogs are involved)
• Covers end-to-end journeys and real plugin behaviour

Golden tests sit alongside widget tests: they render a widget and compare the pixels against a committed reference image, which is how you catch unintended visual changes.

Run them with `flutter test` (unit + widget + golden) and `flutter test integration_test` (on a device).

question: How do you write golden tests in Flutter?
answer:
Golden tests (snapshot tests) compare a widget's rendered output pixel-by-pixel against a saved "golden" reference image. They catch unintended visual regressions.

Workflow:
1. Write test with matchesGoldenFile()
2. Run flutter test --update-goldens to generate reference images
3. Commit the golden files to source control
4. CI runs tests — fails if pixels differ

Gotchas:
• Golden images are platform-dependent (macOS vs Linux vs Windows render slightly differently)
• Run goldens on a fixed platform (usually Linux in CI)
• Swap in a custom `goldenFileComparator` if you need a tolerance for anti-aliasing differences
• For device-size matrices and multi-theme goldens use `alchemist`; golden_toolkit is discontinued

question: How do you test widgets that depend on InheritedWidgets (Theme, MediaQuery, etc.)?
answer:
A widget reading Theme, MediaQuery or Localizations throws in a test unless a scope above it provides them.

So every such test starts by building that scope, and the cheapest way is usually a MaterialApp.

What to wrap in:
• MaterialApp (or CupertinoApp / WidgetsApp) — gives you Theme, Directionality, Localizations, MediaQuery and a Navigator in one line
• A bare MediaQuery only when you need a specific size or text scale and nothing else
• The real state-management scope — ChangeNotifierProvider.value, ProviderScope(overrides: ...), BlocProvider.value — with a fake injected

Changing the environment:
• Screen size and pixel ratio: set `tester.view.physicalSize` and `tester.view.devicePixelRatio`, then `addTearDown(tester.view.reset)` so the next test starts clean
• Text scale: `MediaQuery.withClampedTextScaling`, or a MediaQuery with an explicit `TextScaler`
• Platform: `debugDefaultTargetPlatformOverride`, reset in tearDown

Common dependencies you will have to supply: Theme, MediaQuery (size, orientation, padding), Directionality, Navigator, Localizations, and whatever provider your screen reads.

Write one `pumpApp` helper that builds the standard scope and takes the widget under test. Repeating a ten-line MaterialApp wrapper in forty tests is how test files rot.

question: How do you choose between mocktail and mockito for mocking dependencies?
answer:
Both let you fake classes for tests; the choice mostly comes down to ergonomics and null safety.

mocktail (modern, recommended):
• No code generation — just `class MockX extends Mock implements X {}`
• Works great with sealed classes, records, and Dart 3 features
• Stubbing is closure-based: `when(() => repo.fetch()).thenAnswer((_) async => [...])`
• Forces you to register fallback values for non-nullable arg matchers (`registerFallbackValue(...)`)
• Smaller API surface, less boilerplate

mockito (older, build_runner-based):
• `@GenerateMocks([X])` annotation, `dart run build_runner build` produces `MockX`
• Generated `mocks.mocks.dart` files clutter the test/ directory
• Requires casts and `as Mock` plumbing in places
• Still useful for legacy projects already invested in it

Guidelines:
• New projects → mocktail. Less ceremony, no codegen.
• Mocking concrete classes (not interfaces): mocktail handles it (`class MockDio extends Mock implements Dio {}`); mockito needs `@GenerateNiceMocks([MockSpec<Dio>()])`.
• For TIME and external systems prefer fakes (hand-written stubs implementing the same interface). Mocks should verify CALL CONTRACTS; fakes provide BEHAVIOR.

Common pitfalls regardless of library:
• Stubbing arg matchers without registerFallbackValue → cryptic errors at test run
• Re-stubbing on the same method without `reset()` — old stubs linger
• Mocking too deeply — mocking a Dio Response is brittle; prefer a fake API client

question: What's the difference between pump, pumpAndSettle, pumpFrames, and runAsync in widget tests?
answer:
Widget tests run on a fake clock, so a five-second delay in your code costs the test nothing — you advance time yourself. The pump variants are how you do it.

tester.pump([Duration]):
• Runs the next frame. With no argument, advances 0 ms (just rebuilds).
• With a Duration, advances the clock by that duration and runs intervening frames.
• Use to step through animations frame by frame, or to flush a single setState.

tester.pumpAndSettle([Duration interval]):
• Repeatedly pumps until the binding reports no scheduled frames
• Default `interval: 100ms`; default total timeout: 10 minutes (yes, really)
• Use to skip past a finished animation or wait for the tree to be idle
• Will hang forever on infinite animations (CircularProgressIndicator, repeating Lottie)

tester.pumpFrames(target, maxDuration):
• Pumps frames at a steady interval for a fixed span of time
• Use it for an animation of known length instead of guessing at pumpAndSettle

tester.runAsync<T>(action):
• Executes `action` against the REAL clock. Use it for code that must use a real Future (HTTP-like SDKs, timers under the hood).
• Inside `runAsync`, you cannot call pump — you're outside the test scheduler.
• Required when your code uses `dart:io` HttpClient under the hood, or anything that schedules outside the FakeAsync

Gotchas:
• `pumpAndSettle` near a CircularProgressIndicator hangs — if your loading state shows one, replace with an indeterminate finder before settling, or pump for a fixed duration.
• Network mocks should resolve their Futures via the test scheduler (`Future.value(...)`). Real I/O needs runAsync.

question: How do you write integration tests with integration_test or patrol?
answer:
Integration tests drive the whole app on a real device or emulator, with only the network faked at the boundary. They catch the bugs unit and widget tests structurally cannot.

integration_test (official):
• Same Test API as widget tests, but runs against a real Flutter engine
• Lives in `integration_test/` directory
• `IntegrationTestWidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();` in main
• Run: `flutter test integration_test`
• Limited to Flutter UI — cannot interact with native dialogs, system permissions, push notifications, biometric prompts

patrol (community, more powerful):
• Adds NATIVE control: tap system permission dialogs, type into native text fields, use the system back button reliably, scroll Android settings
• Critical for full E2E flows that touch permissions or share/intent flows
• Uses its own test runner (`patrol test`) that wraps integration_test
• Heavier setup; runs slower than vanilla integration_test

When to use which:
• Pure-Flutter flows — integration_test is enough
• Anything involving permissions, push, share, app settings — patrol
• CI cost matters → keep integration_tests fast, use patrol only for the few E2Es that absolutely need it

Fundamentals (both):
• Replace network with a fake (in-process server, recorded fixtures)
• Wipe storage between tests
• Mock time/date to keep results deterministic
• Tag flakies and run them off the critical path

question: How do you mock HTTP/Dio in tests without real network calls?
answer:
Real HTTP is forbidden in CI — it is flaky, slow, and depends on a staging environment being up. There are three places to cut the wire, from least to most invasive.

1. Inject a fake repository:
• Replace the data source (UsersRepository) with a hand-written fake; the Dio instance is never constructed
• Cleanest separation — the widget test does not know HTTP exists
• Use this whenever you can

2. Mock Dio's adapter:
• Swap `dio.httpClientAdapter` for a controlled adapter (http_mock_adapter's DioAdapter) that matches paths and returns canned responses
• Lets you assert that the right URL, method and body were sent
• Use when the code under test IS the data layer

3. Run a local in-process server:
• Serve `shelf` on a random port and point the base URL at it
• Most realistic — real serialization, real headers, real status codes
• Heavier setup; worth it for integration tests where you want as much real code as possible

Which to use when: fake repository for UI and bloc tests, DioAdapter for repository tests, in-process server for full-flow integration tests.

One gotcha: a test that asserts on `requestOptions.headers` must run the SAME interceptor stack as production. Don't strip the auth interceptor in tests — that is exactly the code you want to verify.

question: How do you measure code coverage and gate it in CI?
answer:
Coverage tells you which lines of source ran during tests. It's a useful indicator and a terrible target — chase covered behaviour, not number-go-up.

Flutter generates `coverage/lcov.info` when you run `flutter test --coverage`. From there:

• Render an HTML report locally with `genhtml` for browsing
• Upload to Codecov / Coveralls — they comment on PRs with diffs
• Gate CI: fail the build if coverage drops below a threshold or the PR adds untested code

What to exclude:
• Generated files (`.g.dart`, `.freezed.dart`, `.gr.dart`) — they don't carry your logic
• `main.dart` boot — usually thin glue with little to test
• Auto-generated GraphQL/protobuf serialization
• Use `// coverage:ignore-line` and `// coverage:ignore-file` annotations sparingly

What to chase:
• Domain logic and reducers (Bloc on<>, Notifier methods) — high value, fast tests
• Error paths — coverage often misses 4xx and 5xx branches; tests there are very valuable
• Pure utility functions — easy to test, easy to break

What to deprioritize:
• 100% widget coverage — golden + integration cover the rendered output more meaningfully
• Trivial getters/setters — no bug surface

CI pattern that works in practice:
• `flutter test --coverage` on PRs
• `dart pub global activate remove_from_coverage` to strip generated files
• Codecov action with a `target: 80%, threshold: 1%` for the diff (a PR can lower coverage by at most 1%)
• Don't fail builds when coverage drops because you wrote a comment — measure the diff, not the absolute
code_example:
# .github/workflows/test.yml
name: Test + Coverage
on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: subosito/flutter-action@v2
        with: { channel: stable }
      - run: flutter pub get
      - run: flutter test --coverage

      # Strip generated files from the report
      - run: |
          dart pub global activate remove_from_coverage
          dart pub global run remove_from_coverage:remove_from_coverage \
            -f coverage/lcov.info \
            -r '\.g\.dart$' \
            -r '\.freezed\.dart$' \
            -r '\.gr\.dart$' \
            -r 'lib/main\.dart$' \
            -r 'lib/generated/.*'

      - name: Upload to Codecov
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v5
        with:
          files: coverage/lcov.info
          fail_ci_if_error: true

# ── Local report ──
# flutter test --coverage
# genhtml coverage/lcov.info -o coverage/html
# open coverage/html/index.html

# ── codecov.yml — gate the diff, not the absolute ──
# coverage:
#   status:
#     project:
#       default:
#         target: auto                  # don't enforce a fixed % 
#         threshold: 1%                  # allow 1% drop max
#     patch:
#       default:
#         target: 80%                    # new code must be >= 80%
# ignore:
#   - lib/main.dart
#   - lib/generated/**
#   - '**/*.g.dart'
#   - '**/*.freezed.dart'

// ── Inline ignores ──
int expensiveCompute(int n) {
  // coverage:ignore-line — debug helper, not worth testing
  if (kDebugMode) print('compute($n)');
  return n * 2;
}

question: How do you test a screen that uses Riverpod or BLoC?
answer:
Both libraries let you swap the dependency layer for fakes and then assert either the emitted state or the rendered UI. The mechanics differ; the shape of the test does not.

Riverpod:
• `ProviderContainer` for unit tests — no widget tree needed
• `overrides:` swaps any provider for a fake (e.g. mock the apiClientProvider, the rest of the graph still composes)
• In widget tests, wrap with `ProviderScope(overrides: [...], child: ...)`
• Pure-Dart logic tests are very fast — no `pumpWidget` overhead

BLoC:
• `blocTest` from package:bloc_test for Bloc/Cubit logic — script events, expect states
• In widget tests, use `BlocProvider.value(value: mockBloc, ...)` to inject
• `MockBloc` and `whenListen(stream, initialState: ...)` simulate state sequences without running the real bloc

Shared rules:
• Test logic in unit tests; test rendering in widget tests; don't test logic by inspecting widgets — slow and brittle
• Reset between tests — fresh ProviderContainer / fresh Bloc / clean storage
• Don't reach into private state. Test the observable behavior (state stream, rendered UI).
• Cancel subscriptions and dispose containers in tearDown to avoid leaks across tests

Both ecosystems play well with mocktail for the dependency layer; use bloc_test specifically for the bloc-flow assertions.

question: In a widget test, how do you prove that tapping a button navigated to the right screen?
answer:
Prefer asserting that the destination is on screen after the tap, and fall back to a mock NavigatorObserver when the destination is too heavy to build.

Asserting the destination:
• Pump a MaterialApp with your routes, tap the button, `pumpAndSettle` to finish the transition, then `expect(find.byType(CheckoutPage), findsOneWidget)`.
• This tests behaviour rather than implementation, so it survives a switch from `Navigator.push` to a named route.
• The destination must be buildable in a test, which usually means its dependencies are injected.

Mock observer:
• Register a `NavigatorObserver` mock in `MaterialApp.navigatorObservers`, then `verify(() => observer.didPush(any(), any()))`.
• With mocktail you must `registerFallbackValue` for `Route` before using `any()`.
• Capture the route to assert on `route.settings.name` or on the widget it builds.
• It couples the test to the Navigator API, so use it when building the destination is expensive.

With go_router:
• Build a `GoRouter` containing only the routes under test and pump `MaterialApp.router`. After settling, either assert the destination widget or read the current location from the router's configuration.
• Redirect logic is worth its own test: drive the router directly and assert where it lands for each auth state.

The design point behind the question:
• A widget that takes an `onContinue` callback instead of calling Navigator itself is trivial to test — you assert the callback fired. Pushing navigation to the edge of the widget makes half of these tests disappear.
• Dialogs and sheets work the same way: they are routes, so assert on their content after pumping, and pump again after dismissing.
• Do not test that Flutter's Navigator works. Test that your widget asks for the right destination.

question: A widget under test calls a plugin and the test throws MissingPluginException. What are your options?
answer:
There is no platform behind a Flutter test, so every channel call has to be answered by a fake — either at the plugin's Dart interface or at the binary messenger.

Best option — replace the plugin's platform interface:
• Modern plugins expose `SomePlugin.instance` or `SomePluginPlatform.instance`, a class you can override with a fake that mixes in `MockPlatformInterfaceMixin`.
• It is typed, it survives channel renames, and it is what plugin authors support.
• Some plugins ship their own helper instead: shared_preferences has `setMockInitialValues`, and several plugins expose a test-only platform implementation.

Fallback — mock the channel itself:
• `TestWidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized()`, then set a handler on `TestDefaultBinaryMessengerBinding.instance.defaultBinaryMessenger`.
• `setMockMethodCallHandler(channel, handler)` for MethodChannel, `setMockStreamHandler` for EventChannel, `setMockMessageHandler` for BasicMessageChannel.
• Calling `setMockMethodCallHandler` directly on the channel object is the old deprecated form; go through the binding.
• Clear the handler in tearDown by passing null, or one test leaks into the next.
• Return exactly the shape the plugin's Dart side decodes, and remember the call is still async — pump afterwards.

The option that removes the problem:
• Wrap the plugin behind your own narrow interface and inject it. Widget tests then use a plain fake and never touch channels, and swapping the package later touches one file.

Whichever you pick, assert on the arguments the plugin received when the call is the point of the test — a mock handler gives you the MethodCall, including its method name and arguments.

question: How do you test a debounce, a retry with backoff, or a poll without making the suite slow?
answer:
Never sleep in a test — run the code against a fake clock and move time forward yourself.

In pure Dart tests:
• Wrap the code in `fakeAsync((async) { ... })` from package:fake_async. Timers and delayed Futures created inside that zone do not fire until you call `async.elapse(...)`.
• `elapse` advances virtual time and runs everything scheduled in between; `flushMicrotasks` drains pending microtasks without moving the clock.
• A three-second debounce and a five-minute backoff both take microseconds, and the test asserts on exact timings instead of hoping.

In widget tests:
• `tester.pump(Duration)` already advances the same kind of fake clock, so you rarely need fake_async there.
• `pumpAndSettle` never returns while a repeating timer or an infinite animation is scheduled; step with explicit `pump(duration)` calls instead.
• Cancel timers in dispose, or the test binding fails the test with a pending-timer error — which is a feature, since it catches a real leak.

Whatever reads the wall clock:
• Do not call `DateTime.now()` deep inside logic. Inject a `DateTime Function()`, or use package:clock and its `clock.now()`, which `withClock` lets tests control.
• The same applies to `Timer` and `Future.delayed` if you need to assert on them from outside the zone: inject the scheduler.

Two traps:
• Real IO cannot run inside fakeAsync — an actual HTTP call or file read will hang, because its completion never arrives on the fake timeline. Fake those dependencies as well.
• Elapsing past several scheduled callbacks runs all of them, so assert the intermediate state by elapsing in the steps you care about.
